 How Do You Choose the Right Amount of Backup Power?
 Start by considering what you want to power during an emergency, like a refrigerator, a computer setup, or the entire house . Or, if you're camping or on a job site, consider the devices you want to power or recharge, such as power tools or camping gear like portable refrigerators .
 Then consider the type of generator or power station you want. Fuel-based generators can run as long as you have enough fuel, but they’re loud and must be run outside because they emit potentially dangerous fumes. Power stations, on the other hand, run virtually silently and don’t emit fumes, so you can run them inside, making them great for city dwellers. They need to be recharged, but you can do that with AC power or a solar panel.

Every discount in this set lands between 34% and 47% off the listing’s regular price, with no coupon or code standing between the reader and the number. Bluetti holds eight of the eleven slots, because that’s where the deep cuts landed this week.
 The list runs in capacity order, smallest first, with the DJI and Anker entries placed where their watt-hours put them. That keeps the price per watt-hour visible as the boxes grow, and the spread runs from 37 cents to just over a dollar. Read the output figure before the capacity figure on every pick, since a big battery behind a small inverter won’t start a kettle.

 1 BLUETTI Elite 10 Mini
 The Elite 10 Mini is the smallest real power station in this set, and it gives up almost nothing a desk or a carry-on bag actually asks for. A 200W AC outlet on a 128Wh battery covers a laptop, a camera charger and a drone case on a workday or a travel day, without pretending it belongs under a refrigerator.
 The listing puts that 200W AC outlet beside a 100W USB-C port and DC outputs on a 4.0-pound box measuring 7.8 by 5.7 by 4.3 inches. The LiFePO4 pack is rated past 3,000 cycles, and a 10-millisecond UPS switchover guards the gear sitting on your desk. A built-in light with three modes rides on top, so the box handles the tent and the nightstand too. At 128Wh it falls inside the 100 to 160Wh band airlines allow in the cabin with prior approval, capped at two per passenger.
 It’s a power bank with a wall outlet attached.

128Wh LiFePO4 · 200W AC outlet · 100W USB-C port · 4.0 lbs · 3 lighting modes

 2 BLUETTI Elite 30 Mini
 Bluetti built the Elite 30 Mini around one small idea, trivial until you’ve packed a bag in the dark: a retractable USB-C cable built into the case. It pulls out to charge, then disappears when the job’s done, so the most-forgotten item in portable power stops being a packing step.
 Under the trick sits a 288Wh LiFePO4 battery rated past 6,000 cycles, two AC outlets, two 140W bidirectional USB-C ports, a 30W USB-C port, a USB-A port and a 12V car outlet. The whole layout rides on a 7.3-pound frame, with an outage switchover under 10 milliseconds so a router never notices the grid dropping. Three lighting modes remember your last brightness setting, finishing the grab-and-go case for the hallway closet.
 The built-in cable sells this one.
 BLUETTI Elite 30 Mini 
288Wh · 300W · retractable USB-C cable
Price: $239.98 $449.00 (save $209.02, 47% off)
Where to buy: Buy on Amazon 
 3 BLUETTI Elite 30 V2
 Same 288Wh capacity as the Mini above, spent differently. The Elite 30 V2 doubles continuous output to 600W and adds a lifting mode rated at 1,500W, moving a small kettle, a toaster or a CPAP machine from the maybe pile into the covered pile.
 Nine output ports spread across the front of a 9.5-pound box measuring 9.8 by 7 by 6.6 inches. The UPS switchover matches the Mini at 10 milliseconds when the power drops mid-storm and the lights go with it. Bluetti’s UltraCell build keeps standby draw low at 4.5W on DC, so a charged unit in a closet isn’t quietly emptying itself between uses. The fifty dollars over the Mini buys output headroom and nothing else, the right trade when your loads include a heating element.
 Buy this over the Mini for heating loads.
 BLUETTI Elite 30 V2 
288Wh LiFePO4 · 600W output, 1,500W lifting · 9 ports · 9.5 lbs
Price: $289.99 $449.00 (save $159.01, 35% off)

 4 DJI Power 1000 V2
 DJI’s entry is the output bully of the 1kWh class here, rated at 2,600W continuous from a 1,024Wh LFP battery where most rivals stop at 1,800W or less. That headroom covers kettles, power tools and a microwave without tripping the inverter, and at $399.98 it undercuts every other 1kWh station in the roundup.
 Two 140W USB-C ports anchor the front panel, and the case runs as low as 26 decibels in quiet operation. The UPS switchover fires in 10 milliseconds when the grid drops under a desk setup. The catch is printed on the listing itself: the MPPT and car charging modules aren’t built in, so solar or vehicle charging takes a separate DJI adapter that isn’t in the box. Anyone planning a solar-first setup should price that adapter in before calling this the cheap option.

 5 BLUETTI Elite 100 Mini
 The Elite 100 Mini stands its kilowatt-hour upright. The tower footprint measures 9.2 by 8.4 inches at the base, so a full 1,004.8Wh of capacity takes less counter, shelf or truck-bed corner than the flat boxes it competes with. It still weighs a manageable 23.5 pounds by the top handle.
 Output is the compromise here, 700W across three AC outlets with a 1,400W surge ceiling, backed by a 140W USB-C port and DC outputs. The UltraCell LiFePO4 pack carries a 6,000-plus cycle rating, the UPS switchover runs at 10 milliseconds, and a built-in light with three modes can light the counter it’s standing on. Shoppers who need a kettle or a microwave running should walk one slot down to the Elite 100 V2 and take its 1,800W instead.

 6 BLUETTI Elite 100 V2
 This is the balanced one in the Bluetti stack, the station in this page’s hero shot, working by the water. A 1,024Wh battery and 1,800W of continuous output with 2,700W of lifting headroom cover the standard camp and outage load list, from the coffee maker to the laptop desk.
 Eleven ports handle the rest of the kit at once, and the LiFePO4 pack is rated past 4,000 cycles. The whole unit weighs 25 pounds in a 12.6 by 8.5 by 9.8 inch case with a hidden handle for one-handed carries. App control over Wi-Fi and Bluetooth covers charging modes, monitoring and firmware from the couch. The UPS switchover holds at 10 milliseconds for the home-office gear it’ll spend most outages protecting. Against the DJI two slots up, it trades raw output for a fuller port spread and built-in charging flexibility.
 The middle of the ladder, done right.

Output peaks higher than the Elite 100 V2 at 2,000W continuous and 3,000W peak across ten ports, giving it the edge when a blender, a kettle and a monitor land on the same strip.
 The app layer is where Anker separates itself here, with a time-of-use mode that schedules charging around peak rates. A 10-millisecond UPS switchover guards the desk while it does so, keeping a dropped grid out of your work. Solar input accepts up to 600W off-grid, the LiFePO4 pack holds at least 80% of its capacity after 4,000 cycles, and the case measures 15.1 by 8.2 by 9.6 inches. The live price also moved in the buyer’s favor, dropping twenty dollars under where this deal first surfaced.
 The desk-first pick of the 1kWh class.
 Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 
1,024Wh · 2,000W output, 3,000W peak · 10 ports · app time-of-use mode
Price: $529.99 $799.00 (save $269.01, 34% off)
Where to buy: Buy on Amazon 
 8 DJI Power 2000
 Step up to two kilowatt-hours and the math in this roundup turns in the buyer’s favor as the output figure climbs with the capacity it carries. The DJI Power 2000 carries 2,048Wh of LFP capacity and a 3,000W output rating, the highest continuous figure in this list, at a price that works out near 37 cents per watt-hour.
 Fifteen ports include dual SDC sockets for DJI’s own fast-charge gear, and the case runs as low as 30 decibels. The UPS switchover matches the smaller DJI at 10 milliseconds for home backup duty. Capacity expands with DJI’s 2,048Wh expansion batteries when the base unit stops being enough, though those batteries sell separately. The footprint is a fixed 17.64 by 8.86 by 12.76 inches wherever it lands. The smaller DJI’s adapter caveat applies here in full: MPPT and car charging modules aren’t built in, so solar and vehicle charging need separate DJI adapters.
 Cheapest capacity in the set, full stop.
 DJI Power 2000 
2,048Wh LFP · 3,000W output · 15 ports incl. dual SDC
Price: $749.99 $1,299.00 (save $549.01, 42% off)
Where to buy: Buy on Amazon 
 9 BLUETTI Elite 200 V2
 Bluetti’s big box answers the DJI directly, with 2,080Wh of capacity and 2,600W of continuous output that lifts to 3,900W for loads that surge at startup. It’s the home-backup pick for shoppers who want the charging hardware built in rather than adapted on, since it takes wall, solar and vehicle power through the case.
 The automotive-grade LiFePO4 pack is rated past 6,000 cycles, and standby draw sits at 10W so more of the charge survives to the loads. It can run nine devices at once across its outlet spread, from the fridge circuit to the phone chargers. UPS switchover runs at 15 milliseconds on this model, a step behind the 10-millisecond figure on the smaller Elites, so sensitive desktop setups should note the difference. For fridge, freezer and workshop duty, that gap never enters the conversation.
 Built-in everything, at the big-box price.
 BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 
2,080Wh · 2,600W output, 3,900W lifting · 6,000+ cycles
Price: $898.99 $1,399.00 (save $500.01, 36% off)
Where to buy: Buy on Amazon 
 10 BLUETTI FridgePower
 One product in this roundup exists for exactly one job, and it’s shaped like it. The FridgePower packs 2,016Wh and 1,800W of output into a slab just 75 millimeters thin, so it slides into the gap behind the refrigerator or mounts on the kitchen wall.
 Standby draw is the spec that sells a fridge battery, and this one sips 4W at idle where conventional stations burn several times that staying awake. The UPS switchover fires in 10 milliseconds when the grid drops, and the app pushes storm alerts ahead of bad weather. Capacity grows to 8,064Wh as BlueCell 200 expansion batteries stack on, for households that lose power for days at a stretch. A separate glance display comes in the box, so the charge state reads from across the kitchen.
 The fridge gets its own battery now.
 BLUETTI FridgePower 
2,016Wh · 1,800W output · 75mm slim, wall-mount ready
Price: $999.00 $1,599.00 (save $600.00, 38% off)
Where to buy: Buy on Amazon 
 11 BLUETTI Charger 1 Alternator Charger (Accessory Pick)
 This one isn’t a power station, and it’s in the roundup because it fixes the weakest link in every station above it. The Charger 1 pulls up to 560W from a vehicle’s alternator while you drive and feeds it to the station in the cargo area. The drive to the trailhead or the cabin stops being dead time for the battery.
 Bluetti rates it for every model in its own line and, by the listing’s count, 95% of third-party power stations, with output adjustable up to 56V. An onboard algorithm watches the vehicle’s starter battery and backs off before the charging load can strand you. An active cooling fan keeps the unit stable in a hot cargo area, and the box includes the 6AWG input cable and installation hardware. It needs a station to feed, which is why it closes the list instead of leading it.
 The road-trip accessory that pays rent.
 BLUETTI Charger 1 
560W alternator charger · 12V/24V input
Price: $218.98 $399.00 (save $180.02, 45% off)
Where to buy: Buy on Amazon 
 How to choose your size
 Match the output figure to the single biggest load first, because a station that can’t start your kettle or your microwave is the wrong station at any capacity. Small boxes under 300W of output belong to phones, laptops, cameras and lights, while the 600W to 2,000W middle covers kitchen and workshop loads one at a time. The 2,600W class and up stops asking which appliance is plugged in.
 Capacity gets cheaper as the boxes get bigger, with the DJI Power 2000 landing near $0.37 per watt-hour while the Elite 30 V2 costs $1.01 for every watt-hour it carries. You’re paying for portability at the small end and getting raw storage at a discount at the big end. Buy the DJI Power 1000 V2 at $399.98 if one box has to split camp and outage duty, and skip the small end entirely if a refrigerator or a heating element is on your list.
 Portable power station deals FAQ
 Are all of these lithium iron phosphate
 Yes, every station in this roundup runs LiFePO4. Cycle ratings on the listings run from 3,000 cycles on the Elite 10 Mini to more than 6,000 on the Elite 30 Mini, Elite 100 Mini and Elite 200 V2. The alternator charger is the exception by design, since it holds no battery of its own.
 Which of these can back up a refrigerator
 The FridgePower is the one built for the job, with its 75mm case shaped for the gap behind the fridge and a 10-millisecond switchover when the grid drops. The two 2kWh stations above it carry the output and capacity for fridge duty as well, and they take the floor space the FridgePower was designed to avoid.
 Do any of these deals need a coupon code
 No, every price in the boxes above is the straight Amazon price on the listing, with no code to enter and no coupon to clip at checkout. The struck-through figure beside each price is that listing’s regular price.

 What to consider before buying the best solar generators 
 Over the past few years, solar generators have exploded onto the market. There are now dozens of different brands that largely look more or less the same at a glance. The fact is, there are only a few standouts among a sea of knockoffs. Here’s what to look for to ensure you’re getting a great one:
 How much power can it store?
 A portable solar generator comes in a wide range of sizes, but a generator’s size doesn’t automatically make it capable of storing a lot of power. In fact, most are disappointingly limited and unable to store much more juice than a portable charger .
 To properly check a generator’s storage, you must look at its capacity, measured in watt-hours (Wh). One watt-hour is the equivalent of 1 watt flowing over the course of an hour. The best solar generators offer capacities of several hundred and sometimes several thousand watt-hours. That doesn’t mean, however, that it will provide power for several hundred or several thousand hours. Any generator will ultimately last a different amount of time, depending on what’s plugged into it.
 It’s easy to predict how long a generator will last when you use it to power one thing. For example, if you were to power a 100-watt bulb using a power station with a capacity of 500 watt-hours, it would stay lit for five continuous hours. Add a portable fridge with a 50W average draw, a phone charger drawing up to 18W, a 3W mini-fan, and runtime drops accordingly. The more capacity, the better.
 Charging capability
 No solar generator will hold a charge forever, so you want one capable of charging as quickly and easily as possible. This is where we put the “renewable” into “renewable energy.”
 All of the power stations included in this roundup can be charged by connecting them to solar panels (hence the designation “solar generators”). Still, you also want to look for the ability to charge via other sources like wall outlets and your vehicle’s 12-volt plug. This ensures that you can charge up whether you’re off-grid in the sun, plugged in while preparing at home, or using your dash socket on the go.
 You must also monitor a model’s charging input capacity, measured in watts (W). For example, a solar-powered generator with a max input of 100W can take in a continuous flow of up to 100 watts, which is about the minimum that you’ll reasonably want to look for. Most of the generators below have input capacities of at least a few hundred watts when charging via solar, so a few 50- to 200-watt solar panels will max them out.
 Output capability
 Solar generators need to keep the power coming in and going out. The best solar generators can simultaneously charge all your intended devices via whatever plugs are necessary.
 Any portable power station worth your money will have a high output capacity so you can charge many devices, even if they require a lot of juice. At a minimum, you’ll want a generator that can put out 300 watts at a time, though you’ll want at least 500 for larger tasks.
 The best solar generators should also offer a variety of output plugs, including AC outlets, USB-A, USB-C, and even 12-volt DC outlets like the one in your vehicle dash. This ensures you can charge several devices simultaneously regardless of their plug. The number of ports you’ll need will vary depending on how many devices you need to power, but it should have at least a couple of AC outlets and enough USB-C and USB-A ports, at suitable wattages, for your devices.
 Portability
 While portable battery sources have been around for a while now, over the past several decades, they’ve been pretty heavy, unwieldy things. One of the most exciting aspects of the latest generation of solar generators is that they’ve become much more physically compact. 
 Suppose you plan on taking a generator camping or working it into a van conversion where every square inch matters; well, size and weight become major considerations. All of the products we’ve recommended are about the size of one or two shoeboxes, three at the most. The lightest weighs about 7 pounds, while the heaviest standalone unit is about 84 pounds. Most fall somewhere between 30 and 60 pounds.
 If you’re using your generator as a more or less stationary source of backup power at home, portability isn’t a huge issue. Still, we generally recommend keeping weight and size in mind; you never know when you’ll need it for something other than a backup. (Plus, who wants to lug around something heavy and awkward if they don’t have to?) 
 Another consideration regarding portability involves the necessity for accessories, which can impact how easy it is to move and use your generator. Some generators, for example, require a lot of removable battery packs, which can be a hassle when you’re on the go or packing a vehicle. All of the picks on our list work on their own, though solar charging requires compatible panels and cables.
 Durability
 As with any product you expect to last, durability and all-around quality craftsmanship are essential. This is especially true if you plan on lugging your generator around on camping and road trips. Many subpar power stations are made from cheap components and flimsy plastic that doesn’t feel like it will hold up under the rigors of the road.
 Durability isn’t something you can determine by reading a spec sheet off the internet. You’ve actually got to take the generator out, use it a bunch, and see how it holds up. I’ve verified the durability of these recommendations via a combination of my own actual field tests and reviews culled from countless real product owners. The Jackery Explorer 2000 v2, Explorer 1000 v2 and Explorer 300 v2 are the exceptions; we haven’t tested them yet.
 Related: Best electric generators 
 FAQs 
 Q: What size solar generator should I get? It’s easy to underestimate how much capacity you need. 1,000 watt-hours might sound like a lot, but if you’re going to power a converted van with a portable fridge, lights, and occasional phone and laptop top-off, that 1,000 watt-hours will go faster than you expect. I used a setup like this and know from personal experience that you should always overestimate how much power you’ll need.
A generator with a capacity under 1,000Wh can keep electronics charged. A larger one with 1,000 to 1,500Wh should be the minimum for road trips where you’ll need it to last multiple days between full charges. For a house or worksite where you expect to use some serious energy, like a full-sized refrigerator or power tools, you’re going to want to start looking at the biggest possible power stations that can be daisy-chained to external batteries.
If you want to get precise, there is an equation :
1. Estimate how many hours you’ll need to power various devices. For example, if you want to power two light bulbs for two hours, you need two hours of operation.
2. Add up the total wattage necessary: the two bulbs are 60 watts each, so you need 120 watts.
3. Multiply these together to find the total watt-hours needed: 2 x 120 = 240Wh. Leave room for conversion losses and a reserve, and you’d want at least a 300Wh solar generator. 
That might sound like a lot for two lightbulbs, but remember that, in most situations, you won’t really be powering 60-watt light bulbs for hours on end. You’ll be charging phones and laptops for an hour here or there, cooling a fridge that kicks on and off every once in a while, using power tools in short bursts, and whatnot.
 Q: How many years will a solar generator last? Power stations are rated in charge cycles, not years. Jackery rates its v2 Explorers for 4,000 cycles before they drop to 70 percent of their original capacity, for example. How many years that adds up to depends on how often you drain and refill the battery, and on storing it within the manufacturer’s temperature range. The best-designed power stations are pretty sturdy, with few to no moving parts, so they should likely keep kicking for a long time, provided that you care for them properly. I’ve been pretty rough with a few of mine, and they show no signs of stopping. 
 Q: Can I run my house on solar power only? Yes and no. While it’s absolutely possible to power your house with solar power, you’re unlikely to do so with a portable solar generator unless you use several at once while limiting your power usage. High-capacity picks such as the Bluetti Apex 300 and EcoFlow Delta 3 Ultra Plus come closest when paired with extra batteries, but how long they last depends on what you run, how much solar you can add, and the weather. Running house circuits, rather than plugging appliances straight into the station, requires a transfer switch or interlock installed by an electrician. Never backfeed power through a wall outlet.

 We’re living in a “golden age” for portable solar generators. When I was a kid, and my family was playing around with solar gear while camping in the ‘90s, the technology couldn’t charge many devices, so it wasn’t all that practical. 
 By contrast, the solar generators I’ve recommended here are incredibly useful. I’ve relied on them to power my work and day-to-day needs while road-tripping nationwide. They’re also great when the power goes out. When a windstorm cut the power at my house for a couple of days, I was still working, watching my stories, and keeping the lights on. 
 We haven’t even scratched the surface in terms of the potential offered by portable, reliable, renewable, relatively affordable power. What we can do now is already incredible. The potential for what may come next, though, is even more exciting.

 Black Friday power station questions
 When are Black Friday and Cyber Monday in 2026?
 Black Friday is Friday, November 27, 2026, and Cyber Monday is Monday, November 30, 2026. Stores often start their sales earlier, and some deals end before the day itself, so every price on this page shows the day we checked it.
 Is the cheapest power station the best deal?
 No. The BLUETTI Elite 30 V2 costs $289.99 and the Dabbsson 600L $299. In independent tests the 600L delivered 653 Wh and the Elite 30 V2 232 Wh, so each usable watt-hour costs $0.46 on the 600L and $1.25 on the Elite 30 V2. The 600L is bigger and heavier (17.6 lb against 9.5 lb), so it isn't the right pick for everyone, but it is the better buy per watt-hour.
 Why don't you show Amazon prices?
 Amazon allows prices only from its own live price feed, and we don't have access to it yet. The Amazon buttons open the listing, where you can see today's price. To compare it with this list, divide the price by the model's usable Wh. Half the models we've priced cost $0.59 or less per usable Wh.
 Are the "regular" prices real?
 We can't tell. Stores set their own regular prices, and we have only recorded prices since early October 2026, so we don't know what each unit usually sells for. That's why we don't show discount percentages. We rank on the price on the day we checked, divided by tested capacity, which works the same whether a unit is on sale or not.
 How often are these prices checked?
 We check each price by hand on the brand's US store, and every card shows the day. The prices on this page were checked on Nov 9, 2026. During the sales, prices and stock can change daily, and some deals need a code at checkout, so check the store before you buy.
 Why isn't a model on this list?
 We rank only models with an independent capacity test and an in-stock store price. When we last checked, the EcoFlow RIVER 3 Plus, UDPower C600, Jackery Explorer 1000 v2, Oscal PowerMax 2400, Pecron E3600LFP, Jackery HomePower 3600 Plus and EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 were sold out on their brand's US store. The DJI Power 1000 V2 has no US brand-store price we could check, and we can't show Amazon prices. Models without an independent test aren't on our site yet.
 What size power station do I need?
 Add up your devices in our run-time calculator , which uses the same tested capacity as this list. For a refrigerator, our fridge guide has tested run times.
 How do we rank the deals?
 Usable Wh is the middle (median) result of each model's counted independent tests: US units at 120 V,
 AC output, loads of 100 W or more. Across all our models that is 63 tests from 
 9 testers.
 Price is the unit-only price on the brand's US store, in stock, checked by hand on the date shown.
 Where the brand's own store doesn't sell a model, the card names the US dealer we checked.
 Cost per usable Wh is the price divided by usable Wh. Lower is better.
 The verdict is our own rule: Great value at 50¢ or less, Good value up to 60¢, Fair price up to 75¢, Pricey above that.

 Skip the bundle if your outages last hours rather than days, because you may never unfold the panels. Our guide to portable power stations vs generators helps you work out how long an outage you are planning for.

 Start with what you want to run. Add up the watts of everything you want on at the same time, then choose a unit with at least that much output. Our guide to what size power station you need for a refrigerator shows the math for the most common load.

 Buy for stock, not just price. On November 12, four of the eight units here were sold out and two more ship in December. If you need power for winter storms, an in-stock unit at a slightly higher price beats a lower price that arrives after the storm.
 Who should skip these Black Friday deals
 Skip them if your needs are small: phones, a router and a lamp do not need a 1 kWh station. Skip them if you want a whole-home system; those prices depend on the panel and installation, and a percentage off the box matters less than the electrician’s quote.  Usual

 The lowest price we have read on the maker’s own store since July 17 . Discounts applied automatically count; typed coupon codes and marketplace listings do not.

 Black Friday power station questions
 When is Black Friday 2026?
 + Black Friday 2026 is November 27, and Cyber Monday is November 30. Power station sales usually run well beyond those two days, so this page covers the whole stretch and re-reads every store twice a day.
 When do Black Friday power station sales start?
 + Not on a fixed day. In the months we have tracked, discounts arrived in waves, a brand at a time: on Oct 11 Anker put 7 units on sale in a single day. This page re-reads every store twice a day, so a new sale shows here within about 12 hours of starting.
 Do power stations go on sale before Black Friday?
 + Yes. In 2025 the earliest Black Friday sale we found was EcoFlow's, starting November 4 with up to 80% off. Early prices are not always the lowest, which is why each unit's price to beat is on this page.
 Is Black Friday the cheapest time to buy a power station?
 + Not automatically. The price-to-beat column is the lowest price each unit has sold for at its maker's store since July 17. Today 31 units sell for more than 5% above a price they have already had. If a Black Friday price does not beat that number, it is a sale you could have had on an ordinary week.
 How do you know a discount is real?
 + We compare today's price with the price the unit actually sold for on most days over the last 90, read by us from the maker's store twice a day. We never use the store's crossed-out "was" price: today 28 of the units we track show one higher than anything we have ever seen them sell for.
 Should I wait for a lower price?
 + Only if today's price is above the price to beat. Discounts are short: of the 78 sales we watched start and finish, half lasted 4 days or less. A unit at its lowest recorded price is unlikely to get much cheaper soon.
 Why is a unit I want missing from the deals?
 + It is at its usual price, out of stock, or too new to judge (we need a few weeks of prices before we know what "usual" is). Every unit we track is in the price-to-beat table with its status.
 Do you earn money from these links?
 + Some stores pay us a commission when you buy through our links, at no cost to you. It never changes the order: deals are ranked by how far each unit is under its own usual price.
 Should I buy on Amazon or from the brand's own store?
 + Either can be cheaper on a given day. Every price on this page is read from the maker's own store, where the "usual" and "lowest" figures come from. If Amazon shows a lower price, check that the unit is sold by Amazon or the brand's official storefront, and compare the return window before you buy.
 What is a good Black Friday price for a portable power station?
 + A good price is one under that unit's own price to beat, the lowest we have recorded for it. As a yardstick, the best value on this page today is the Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2 at $0.46 per watt-hour. Compare dollars per watt-hour only between units of the same battery chemistry.
